title: Infectious Diseases of the Lungs and Upper Respiratory Tract
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers infections of the lung and airways: bacterial, atypical, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral pneumonias, lung abscess and aspiration, the toxin diseases diphtheria and pertussis, infant bronchiolitis, and zoonotic and bioterrorism pneumonias. Board questions usually give a host, an exposure, and an imaging or tissue pattern and ask for the organism, or give the organism and ask for the complication. Three questions organize most answers: where the organism lands and spreads (alveolar space, bronchiole, or interstitium), which defense controls it (antibody and neutrophils, or Th1 cells and macrophages), and whether a toxin acts far from the infection. The biology of each pathogen is taught in PU-13; this chapter applies it to disease.

blocks.text: Pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma in which exudate fills alveoli. Its gross pattern depends on where the organism starts and how the exudate spreads. In lobar pneumonia, organisms deposited in distal airspaces provoke a protein-rich edema fluid that carries them through the pores of Kohn and small airways into neighboring alveoli, so a large part of a lobe, or the whole lobe, consolidates at once. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes most cases; its polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis until antibody and complement opsonize it. Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a similar pattern in people with alcohol use disorder, diabetes, or aspiration risk, often in an upper lobe; its thick capsule and the necrosis it causes produce mucoid, blood-tinged currant jelly sputum, and abscess is common.

Untreated lobar pneumonia passes through four stages that follow the course of acute inflammation. The pleura over the lobe is usually inflamed (fibrinous pleuritis), which causes pleuritic chest pain and can lead to effusion or empyema.

blocks.title: Stages of lobar pneumonia
steps: Congestion: engorged capillaries, edema fluid, many bacteria, few neutrophils
Red hepatization: neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin fill alveoli
Gray hepatization: red cells break down, fibrinosuppurative exudate persists
Resolution: enzymes digest exudate, macrophages clear debris, architecture restored
blocks.caption: Classically about 1 to 2 days for congestion, then several days each for the hepatization stages; timing is approximate and shortened by treatment.

blocks.text: Consolidated lung is airless but solid, and solid tissue transmits sound and vibration better than aerated lung. That single fact explains the exam: dullness to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, egophony (spoken "ee" heard as "ay"), and whispered pectoriloquy, often with crackles. The filled alveoli are still perfused, so blood passes them without gas exchange; this right-to-left shunt causes hypoxemia that improves only partly with supplemental oxygen.

Bronchopneumonia begins in bronchioles and spreads to the alveoli around each one, producing scattered patchy foci of consolidation, often bilateral and basal. Typical causes are Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and other gram-negative rods; it is common in infants, older adults, and hospitalized or debilitated patients. Because the consolidated areas are small and separated by aerated lung, the classic consolidation signs are often absent, and crackles over several areas are the main finding.

blocks.predict: A patient with right lower lobe consolidation breathes 100% oxygen. Will the arterial PO2 rise to normal?
blocks.explain: Only partly. Blood flowing through the consolidated lobe never meets alveolar gas, so added oxygen cannot reach it; the shunted blood keeps arterial PO2 low.

sections.title: Atypical pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella, and viruses

blocks.text: Atypical pneumonia is defined by its pattern rather than one organism. The inflammation sits mainly in the alveolar septa, which fill with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, while the alveolar spaces stay relatively free of exudate. Patients have a gradual illness with low-grade fever, headache, myalgia, sore throat, and a dry or scantily productive cough. Because little exudate reaches the airspaces, sputum is scant, Gram stain shows no dominant organism, and focal consolidation signs are usually absent. The chest radiograph nevertheless shows patchy or reticular interstitial infiltrates, often in several areas, so the film looks worse than the patient ("walking pneumonia").

Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the classic cause in school-age children and young adults in close quarters such as dormitories, barracks, and households. It has no cell wall: it lacks peptidoglycan and has sterols in its membrane, so it does not Gram stain and has no target for beta-lactam drugs. A terminal adhesin protein (P1) binds ciliated respiratory epithelium, where the organism damages cells and stops ciliary beating, causing a persistent cough. About half of patients form cold agglutinins, IgM antibodies against the I antigen on red cells that bind best below body temperature and fix complement, which can cause hemolysis. Other extrapulmonary effects include erythema multiforme and bullous myringitis.

Chlamydia pneumoniae (also called Chlamydophila pneumoniae) is an obligate intracellular bacterium that causes a mild, prolonged illness, often with pharyngitis and hoarseness. Respiratory viruses, including influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza, and coronaviruses, produce the same interstitial pattern.

Legionella pneumophila is a gram-negative rod that stains poorly with Gram stain and lives in warm water inside amoebae. People inhale aerosols from cooling towers, hot tubs, showers, and plumbing; it does not spread person to person. Inside alveolar macrophages it blocks phagolysosome fusion. Legionnaires disease often affects older smokers, people with chronic lung disease, and the immunosuppressed, and is more severe than other atypical pneumonias: high fever, confusion, diarrhea, hyponatremia, and sometimes abnormal liver tests. Its radiograph may show consolidation, so it is atypical in organism more than in pattern. Legionella needs buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron, and a urinary antigen test detects serogroup 1.

Obligate intracellular; elementary and reticulate bodies

sections.title: Diphtheria: local pseudomembrane and distant toxin injury

blocks.text: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a gram-positive, club-shaped rod that colonizes the pharynx, tonsils, larynx, or skin and does not usually invade deeper tissue. Disease is caused by diphtheria toxin, whose gene (tox) is carried by a lysogenic beta-prophage. Only strains carrying the phage are toxigenic, and the iron-dependent repressor DtxR blocks toxin production until iron becomes scarce. The toxin is an A-B toxin: the B portion binds the heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor precursor on host cells and the A fragment enters the cytoplasm and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2). Protein synthesis stops and the cell dies.

blocks.title: From colonization to distant toxin injury
steps: Toxigenic strain colonizes the pharynx or tonsils
Toxin kills epithelial cells; fibrin and leukocytes accumulate
Gray adherent pseudomembrane forms; bleeds when scraped
Local edema and cervical nodes produce bull neck
Absorbed toxin travels in blood
Myocardium: myocarditis, conduction block, arrhythmia
Nerves: palatal and cranial palsies, later demyelinating polyneuropathy
blocks.caption: The local lesion and the systemic damage come from the same toxin acting at different sites.

blocks.text: Local cell death produces the pseudomembrane, a tough gray layer of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, leukocytes, red cells, and bacteria that is firmly attached to the underlying mucosa, so removing it leaves a bleeding surface. This adherence separates it from the easily wiped exudate of streptococcal or viral tonsillitis. The membrane can extend into the larynx and trachea and obstruct the airway, or detach and be aspirated. Marked cervical lymphadenopathy with soft tissue edema gives the swollen bull neck of severe disease. Fever is usually low grade.

Toxin absorbed into the blood damages organs far from the throat, chiefly the heart and nerves, and the size of the local lesion roughly predicts the amount of toxin absorbed. Myocarditis usually appears in the first or second week, causing ST and T wave changes, AV block or bundle branch block, arrhythmias, and heart failure; it is the main cause of death. Neuropathy is demyelinating and appears in sequence: palatal paralysis with nasal speech and regurgitation of fluids within the first weeks, then other cranial nerve palsies such as loss of accommodation, then a peripheral polyneuropathy weeks later. Because damage comes from protein synthesis arrest rather than tissue invasion, recovery is usually slow but complete in survivors.

The organism grows on Loeffler medium, where methylene blue shows metachromatic (volutin) granules, and on cystine-tellurite agar, where it reduces tellurite to form gray to black colonies. Since nontoxigenic strains exist, toxin production must be proved, classically by the Elek test, an immunodiffusion test in which toxin from the isolate and antitoxin form a precipitin line in the agar; PCR can detect the tox gene.

sections.title: Endemic fungal pneumonia in healthy hosts

blocks.text: Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, and Coccidioides immitis and posadasii are thermally dimorphic fungi. In soil they grow as molds that release airborne conidia; at about 37 °C (98.6 °F) in the lung they convert to yeasts or, for Coccidioides, spherules. Unlike Aspergillus or Pneumocystis, they infect people with normal immunity, and geography and exposure point to the organism.

The tissue forms resist killing by neutrophils, so control depends on cell-mediated immunity, the same mechanism that controls tuberculosis. Dendritic cells and macrophages present fungal antigen and secrete IL-12, Th1 cells release interferon-gamma that activates macrophages, and TNF-alpha organizes granulomas. Most healthy hosts have mild or no illness and heal with granulomas that may caseate, fibrose, and calcify. The result mimics tuberculosis: necrotizing granulomas, calcified lung nodules and hilar or mediastinal nodes, and sometimes chronic cavitary upper lobe disease, especially in people with emphysema. Histologic stains for fungi (methenamine silver, periodic acid-Schiff) and the shape of the organism make the distinction.

blocks.caption: All three form granulomas that can mimic tuberculosis on imaging and in tissue.

blocks.text: Dissemination occurs when cell-mediated immunity fails to contain the primary focus. Risk rises with HIV infection, organ transplantation, glucocorticoids, and TNF-alpha inhibitors, which weaken the Th1 and granuloma response. Coccidioides also disseminates more often in people of Filipino or African ancestry and in pregnancy, especially the third trimester. Disseminated disease reaches the skin, bones and joints, and meninges; Histoplasma favors macrophage-rich organs because it lives inside macrophages. Erythema nodosum in valley fever is a hypersensitivity reaction and signals a strong cell-mediated response, not spread of the organism.

sections.title: Pneumocystis pneumonia versus the forms of aspergillosis

blocks.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an atypical fungus that cannot be cultured routinely. It is acquired by inhalation, is common in healthy people without disease, and attaches to type I pneumocytes. Control requires CD4 T cells, which direct alveolar macrophages to clear it, so pneumonia occurs when the CD4 count falls below about 200 cells per microliter in HIV infection, and with high-dose glucocorticoids, transplantation, and some cancers. The alveoli fill with a foamy, eosinophilic exudate made of organisms and protein, and the alveolar septa thicken with interstitial inflammation.

Onset in HIV is subacute over weeks: fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea on exertion. The radiograph shows bilateral, diffuse, often perihilar ground-glass opacities, and cysts may form and rupture to cause pneumothorax. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is elevated by lung injury, a sensitive but nonspecific clue. Diagnosis is by finding cysts with methenamine silver or immunofluorescent stain in induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid; serum beta-D-glucan supports it.

blocks.title: Why oxygen saturation falls with exertion
blocks.text: At rest, red cells spend about 0.75 s in a pulmonary capillary and normally reach equilibrium with alveolar gas in about the first third of that time. In Pneumocystis pneumonia, exudate and septal thickening slow oxygen diffusion, so equilibrium takes longer but can still be reached at rest, and resting saturation may be near normal. During exercise, cardiac output rises and transit time can fall to about 0.25 s. Blood now leaves the capillary before it is fully oxygenated, the A-a gradient widens, and saturation drops. A fall in saturation on walking with a normal resting value is therefore a sign of diffusion limitation.

Aspergillus fumigatus is a mold with septate hyphae that branch at acute angles. Its small conidia are inhaled by everyone; alveolar macrophages kill conidia and neutrophils kill hyphae. Disease depends on the host: an old cavity, absent neutrophils, or an allergic airway.

blocks.predict: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a neutrophil count near zero for three weeks and develops fever, hemoptysis, and a lung nodule with a ground-glass halo. Is the CD4 count the key risk?
blocks.explain: No. Neutrophils kill Aspergillus hyphae, so prolonged neutropenia allows angioinvasion; the halo is hemorrhage around an infarcted nodule. CD4 failure is the main risk for Pneumocystis.

blocks.text: A lung abscess is a localized area of suppurative necrosis that forms a cavity in the lung. The most common route is aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions. Normally the cough and gag reflexes and closure of the glottis keep these secretions out of the lower airway. Aspiration becomes likely when consciousness is reduced (alcohol intoxication, seizures, general anesthesia, drug overdose) or swallowing is impaired (stroke, neuromuscular disease, esophageal disorders). Poor dental hygiene and periodontal disease raise the number of anaerobes in each aspirated drop, which is why abscess is uncommon in people without teeth.

The organisms are mixed oral anaerobes, mainly Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella and oral Bacteroides species, and Fusobacterium, often with microaerophilic streptococci. They cause liquefactive necrosis over one to two weeks. When the necrotic center drains into a bronchus, air enters the cavity and the radiograph shows a cavity with an air-fluid level. Anaerobic metabolism produces foul-smelling short-chain fatty acids and sulfur compounds, so the sputum and breath are putrid. The illness is usually subacute, with fever, cough, weight loss, and night sweats over weeks, and clubbing may develop if it persists. Complications include rupture into the pleural space (empyema), hemorrhage, and septic spread to the brain.

The site follows gravity and the anatomy of the bronchial tree. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, so aspirated material more often enters the right lung. In a person lying supine, it flows into the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the superior segment of the lower lobe; in an upright person, it falls to the basal segments of the lower lobe.

Not every cavity is anaerobic. Staphylococcus aureus causes necrotizing pneumonia with abscesses, often after influenza, and septic emboli from right-sided endocarditis in people who inject drugs produce multiple cavitating nodules. Klebsiella causes necrotizing upper lobe pneumonia in people with alcohol use disorder or diabetes. Other causes of a cavity to keep in mind are an abscess behind a bronchus obstructed by carcinoma (suspect in an older smoker), tuberculosis, endemic fungi, and a cavitating squamous cell carcinoma itself.

sections.title: Pertussis: stages, lymphocytosis, and infant disease

blocks.text: Bordetella pertussis is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium with filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae. It stays on the epithelial surface and causes disease through toxins. Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the inhibitory G protein (Gi), so Gi can no longer restrain adenylate cyclase and cAMP rises in many cell types. Adenylate cyclase toxin enters phagocytes and makes cAMP directly, weakening their killing. Tracheal cytotoxin, a fragment of peptidoglycan, kills ciliated cells, so mucus and debris accumulate in the airways. Spread is by respiratory droplets, and the disease is highly contagious.

blocks.title: Clinical stages of pertussis
rows: Rhinorrhea, mild cough, low-grade fever; most contagious; culture most often positive
Bursts of rapid coughs on one breath, then an inspiratory whoop; posttussive vomiting, cyanosis, exhaustion; well between attacks
Ciliated cells lost; mucus pools and triggers cough; toxin effects peak
Paroxysms gradually lessen; may return with later viral infections
blocks.caption: The whoop is a forceful inspiration through a narrowed glottis after the coughing burst empties the lungs.

blocks.text: A marked absolute lymphocytosis is typical, often with a total white cell count well above normal. The mechanism is that lymphocytes leave the blood in response to chemokines, whose receptors signal through Gi. When pertussis toxin disables Gi, lymphocytes cannot migrate into lymph nodes and tissues, so they accumulate in the circulation. Very high counts in young infants are associated with pulmonary hypertension and a worse outcome.

Pertussis is most dangerous in infants younger than about 6 months, especially those too young to be fully immunized. They often do not whoop, because they cannot generate a forceful inspiration; instead they gag, turn cyanotic, or have apnea. Pneumonia, from Bordetella itself or secondary bacteria, is the most common cause of death, and hypoxia can cause seizures and encephalopathy. Adolescents and adults, whose vaccine immunity has waned, often have only a prolonged cough without a whoop and serve as a source for infants. The force of the paroxysms explains other complications: subconjunctival hemorrhage, rib fracture, pneumothorax, and hernia.

Diagnosis uses nasopharyngeal PCR or culture on Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium, and culture is most likely to be positive early, before the typical cough is recognized. The fall in positivity later explains why a child in the paroxysmal stage may have a negative culture.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus long grouped with the paramyxoviruses and now placed in the pneumovirus family. Its G protein attaches to respiratory epithelium and its F (fusion) protein fuses infected cells with neighbors, forming the multinucleated syncytia that give the virus its name; it has no hemagglutinin or neuraminidase. Nearly all children are infected by about age 2, and immunity is incomplete, so reinfection occurs throughout life, usually as a cold. In temperate climates, epidemics occur each winter, roughly from late fall to early spring.

RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and of viral pneumonia in infants, with hospitalization peaking in the first months of life. Infection begins in the nose and spreads to the bronchiolar epithelium over a few days. Infected cells become necrotic and slough, lymphocytes infiltrate around the bronchioles, the submucosa swells, and mucus mixes with cell debris to form plugs.

blocks.title: From bronchiolar injury to hypoxemia
steps: RSV infects and kills bronchiolar epithelial cells
Edema, mucus, and debris narrow small bronchioles
Airway resistance rises steeply in tiny infant airways
Partial plugs trap air: hyperinflation and wheeze
Complete plugs absorb distal gas: patchy atelectasis
Ventilation and perfusion mismatch causes hypoxemia
blocks.caption: Small airway radius, not alveolar filling, drives most of the disease.

blocks.text: Infant bronchioles have a very small radius, and resistance to laminar flow varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius, so a thin layer of edema and mucus raises resistance far more than it would in an adult. Air can pass a partial plug on inspiration, when airways widen, but is trapped on expiration, when they narrow; this produces hyperinflation and expiratory wheeze. The illness starts with rhinorrhea and cough and progresses over a few days to tachypnea, wheezing, fine crackles, nasal flaring, and intercostal retractions. Very young and premature infants may present with apnea before other signs.

Severe disease is most likely in infants born prematurely, who have small airways, little maternal antibody (most IgG crosses the placenta late in pregnancy), and often chronic lung disease of prematurity; in those with hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, especially lesions with increased pulmonary blood flow or pulmonary hypertension, which leave little cardiopulmonary reserve; and in those with chronic lung disease, immunodeficiency, or neuromuscular weakness. RSV also causes serious lower respiratory infection in older adults and the immunocompromised. Diagnosis, when needed, is by antigen or PCR testing of nasopharyngeal secretions.

sections.title: Primary tuberculosis, latent infection, and tuberculosis testing

blocks.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads in droplet nuclei, particles about 1 to 5 um across that stay suspended in air and reach the alveoli. Primary tuberculosis is infection in a person never exposed before. Inhaled bacilli land where ventilation is greatest, typically in the lower part of an upper lobe or the upper part of a lower lobe, close to the pleura. Alveolar macrophages ingest them, but the organism blocks phagosome maturation and fusion with lysosomes, so it multiplies inside the cells and travels in lymphatics to hilar nodes and often briefly into the blood.

blocks.title: Primary infection to latency
steps: Droplet nuclei deliver bacilli to subpleural alveoli
Bacilli multiply in macrophages; spread to hilar nodes
About 3 weeks: IL-12 drives Th1 cells
Interferon-gamma activates macrophages to kill bacilli
Epithelioid granulomas with caseous centers form; TNF-alpha maintains them
Ghon focus and hilar node heal by fibrosis and calcification
Viable bacilli persist: latent infection
blocks.caption: The same cell-mediated response that contains the bacilli produces the tuberculin reaction and caseous necrosis.

blocks.text: The parenchymal lesion, about 1 to 1.5 cm of gray-white consolidation with central caseation, is the Ghon focus; with the involved hilar nodes it forms the Ghon complex, which after fibrosis and calcification is called a Ranke complex. Granulomas contain epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells around caseous necrosis. In most people this response contains the infection with few or no symptoms, leaving latent tuberculosis infection: viable but controlled bacilli, no symptoms, and no transmission. Without treatment, the lifetime risk of reactivation is about 5 to 10% in immunocompetent people and much higher with HIV. In young children and the immunosuppressed, primary infection may instead progress directly to pneumonia, miliary disease, or meningitis (progressive primary tuberculosis).

The tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) injects purified protein derivative (PPD) intradermally; sensitized T cells recruit macrophages over 48 to 72 hours, producing induration, a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Induration, not redness, is measured, and the cutoff depends on risk: about 5 mm in HIV infection, recent close contacts, and the immunosuppressed; about 10 mm in other higher-risk groups; and about 15 mm with no risk factors. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) instead use antigens absent from BCG.

blocks.title: Interpreting tuberculosis immune tests
rows: T cell interferon-gamma response to ESAT-6 and CFP-10
Rarely, except a few species (for example M. kansasii, M. marinum)
HIV, steroids, malnutrition, sarcoidosis, overwhelming tuberculosis, infection under about 8 weeks old
Same causes of weak T cell response

blocks.title: Reading a tuberculin skin test
blocks.text: A 30-year-old woman who moved from a country with high tuberculosis prevalence 2 years ago, and who received BCG in infancy, has 12 mm of induration at 72 hours on screening. Step 1: recent arrival from a high-prevalence country places her in the 10 mm group, so the test is positive. Step 2: BCG can cause a positive skin test, so the result may not mean infection. Step 3: an IGRA uses antigens absent from BCG; a positive IGRA supports true infection, while a negative one points to a BCG effect. Step 4: neither test shows activity; a chest radiograph and, if abnormal or symptomatic, sputum testing decide between latent and active tuberculosis.

blocks.predict: A patient with advanced HIV and a CD4 count of 50 cells per microliter has active tuberculosis but 0 mm of induration on a tuberculin skin test. Why?
blocks.explain: The skin reaction needs CD4 Th1 cells to recruit and activate macrophages. Without them there is no induration even with active infection, an example of anergy.
blocks.check: Compare with the false negative row of the testing table.

blocks.text: Secondary tuberculosis arises in a person already sensitized, usually by reactivation of latent bacilli when cell-mediated immunity weakens, and sometimes by reinfection. It favors the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes. M. tuberculosis is a strict aerobe, and the apices have the highest ventilation to perfusion ratio in upright lungs, so alveolar PO2 there is highest; reduced lymphatic flow at the apices may also contribute.

Because the host is already sensitized, the response is rapid and destructive. Caseous necrosis enlarges and liquefies, and when it erodes into a bronchus the contents are coughed out, leaving a cavity. Cavities contain enormous numbers of bacilli in a well-oxygenated space, which makes these patients highly infectious and spreads infection along the airways to other parts of the lung. Erosion of vessels in the cavity wall causes hemoptysis, occasionally massive from a dilated pulmonary artery branch (Rasmussen aneurysm). Healing produces fibrosis that retracts the upper lobes.

The systemic symptoms come from cytokines, not from the bacillus directly. TNF-alpha and IL-1 from activated macrophages act on the hypothalamus to cause fever, often in the evening with drenching night sweats, and TNF-alpha (also called cachectin) promotes the loss of appetite, muscle, and fat that causes weight loss. Chronic productive cough, fatigue, and hemoptysis complete the picture. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli, nucleic acid amplification, and culture confirm the diagnosis.

Miliary tuberculosis results when bacilli enter the bloodstream in large numbers, from a primary or secondary focus, and seed many organs with lesions about 2 mm across that resemble millet seeds. Erosion into pulmonary arteries or lymphatics seeds the lungs, while spread into pulmonary veins and the systemic circulation seeds other organs. Extrapulmonary disease can also appear years after silent seeding during primary infection.

blocks.title: Major extrapulmonary sites of tuberculosis
rows: Basilar meningitis with cranial nerve palsies, high protein, low glucose, lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid
Pott disease: thoracolumbar vertebral bodies and discs collapse anteriorly, causing kyphosis (gibbus) and sometimes psoas abscess or cord compression
Sterile pyuria (white cells with negative routine culture), hematuria
Bilateral destruction causing primary adrenal insufficiency
blocks.caption: Extrapulmonary disease is more common with HIV and in young children.

blocks.text: Risk of reactivation and dissemination rises whenever Th1 immunity or granuloma maintenance fails: HIV (the strongest risk factor), TNF-alpha inhibitors (which dissolve granulomas), glucocorticoids, transplantation, diabetes mellitus, silicosis, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, and older age. In advanced HIV, too few CD4 cells remain to form organized granulomas, so tuberculosis often looks like primary disease, with lower or middle lobe infiltrates, hilar nodes, few cavities, and more extrapulmonary and miliary disease.

sections.title: Coronaviruses: common colds, SARS, MERS, and COVID-19

blocks.text: Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with large genomes (about 30 kb) and club-shaped spike proteins that form a crown on electron microscopy. Four endemic human strains (229E, OC43, NL63, and HKU1) cause common colds, mostly in winter, and a minority of lower respiratory infections. Three strains that crossed from animals caused severe pneumonia: SARS-CoV (2002 to 2003), MERS-CoV (from 2012, Arabian Peninsula, linked to dromedary camels, binding dipeptidyl peptidase 4), and SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19 (from late 2019).

SARS-CoV-2 spike binds angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), expressed on nasal ciliated and goblet cells, type II pneumocytes, vascular endothelium, and intestinal epithelium. Before fusion the spike must be cleaved, at the cell surface by the host protease TMPRSS2 or inside endosomes by cathepsins. High ACE2 expression in the nose favors early upper airway replication and spread before or without symptoms. Loss of smell results mainly from infection of the supporting (sustentacular) cells of the olfactory epithelium, which express ACE2, rather than of olfactory neurons, which helps explain why smell usually returns.

Most infections cause a mild upper respiratory illness. In a minority, disease progresses in the second week to pneumonia with bilateral, peripheral, lower zone ground-glass opacities. The lung shows diffuse alveolar damage, the tissue pattern of ARDS: injured type I and II pneumocytes, protein-rich edema, and hyaline membranes, followed by an organizing phase. Endothelial injury, complement activation, and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 make the blood hypercoagulable; D-dimer rises, and microthrombi in alveolar capillaries and venous and arterial thrombosis elsewhere are common in severe cases. Lymphopenia is typical.

Older age is the strongest risk factor for severe disease and death. Others include obesity, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, and immunosuppression, together with male sex. Children usually have mild illness, but a few develop a delayed multisystem inflammatory syndrome weeks after infection. SARS and MERS caused similar diffuse alveolar damage with higher case fatality, but transmission occurred mainly after symptoms began, often in hospitals, which made them easier to contain.

Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not incubating at admission; ventilator-associated pneumonia develops 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation. The organisms differ from community-acquired pneumonia because the host and the route differ. Within days of serious illness, the oropharynx becomes colonized by gram-negative rods, partly because epithelial cells lose surface fibronectin that normally favors gram-positive flora. Raising gastric pH with acid suppression allows gastric colonization as well. These secretions are then microaspirated.

An endotracheal tube bypasses the nose, glottis, and cough, carries organisms in a biofilm on its surface, and allows secretions pooled above the cuff to leak into the trachea. Sedation and lying flat add to aspiration. The usual organisms are Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus including methicillin-resistant strains (MRSA), and enteric gram-negative rods such as Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, and Serratia, with Acinetobacter in some units. Multidrug resistance and severe underlying illness give these pneumonias a high mortality. Pseudomonas also stands out in cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and neutropenia.

Aspiration covers two different processes that boards ask you to separate. Chemical aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) is acute lung injury from inhaled acidic gastric contents, typically during anesthesia, drug overdose, or seizure in a person with a full stomach. Acid burns the airway and alveolar epithelium and the injury is initially sterile; dyspnea, wheeze, hypoxemia, and infiltrates in dependent segments appear within hours. It may resolve within a day or two or progress to ARDS. Bacterial aspiration pneumonia is infection by oropharyngeal bacteria in a person with dysphagia or reduced consciousness, often with poor dentition. It develops over days with fever, cough, and an infiltrate in a dependent segment and can progress to lung abscess and empyema (C06).

sections.title: Influenza pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, and new strains

blocks.text: Influenza viruses are enveloped orthomyxoviruses with a negative-sense RNA genome in eight separate segments. Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium to start infection, and neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions. The virus destroys ciliated columnar cells of the trachea and bronchi, causing necrotizing tracheobronchitis and loss of mucociliary clearance; regrowth of epithelium takes about two weeks or more.

Primary influenza pneumonia occurs when the virus reaches the alveoli. It causes interstitial inflammation and diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes and can progress quickly to ARDS. Risk is highest in older adults, pregnancy, and people with heart or lung disease. Secondary bacterial pneumonia is more common and follows a typical sequence: the patient improves after the viral illness, then, often within the first two weeks, relapses with new fever, productive cough, and consolidation.

blocks.title: Influenza opens the door to bacteria
steps: Influenza kills ciliated airway epithelium
Mucociliary clearance fails; basement membrane exposed
Neuraminidase exposes receptors used by bacteria
Viral infection impairs macrophage and neutrophil killing
S. aureus or S. pneumoniae adhere and invade
Relapse with consolidation; necrotizing pneumonia with S. aureus
blocks.caption: H. influenzae and Streptococcus pyogenes are less common causes of postinfluenza pneumonia.

blocks.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most common secondary pathogen, but Staphylococcus aureus is characteristic of postinfluenza pneumonia and is often necrotizing, with cavities, hemoptysis, and rapid deterioration; strains producing Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a toxin that lyses leukocytes, are especially destructive.

Influenza A infects wild waterfowl, the natural reservoir, as well as poultry, pigs, and humans, while influenza B is essentially human only. Antigenic drift is gradual point mutation in hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes, causing yearly epidemics. Antigenic shift occurs when two influenza A strains infect the same cell and package each other's segments (reassortment), producing a new hemagglutinin or neuraminidase subtype to which the population has no immunity and which can cause a pandemic. Human-adapted strains prefer sialic acid in alpha-2,6 linkage, abundant in the upper airway; avian strains prefer alpha-2,3 linkage, found in birds and deeper in the human lung. Pigs carry both types, so they can be co-infected and act as mixing vessels. This receptor difference explains why avian strains such as H5N1 rarely infect humans and spread poorly between them, but cause severe lower respiratory disease when they do.

blocks.title: Antigenic drift and antigenic shift
rows: Point mutations in HA and NA genes
New HA or NA subtype; little or no immunity
blocks.caption: Shift requires a segmented genome and an animal reservoir, which is why only influenza A shifts.

blocks.text: Several zoonotic organisms cause pneumonia when inhaled, and some are listed as potential bioterrorism agents because they are infectious by aerosol at low doses. The key to each is the exposure history, and the key to anthrax is that the lesion is in the mediastinum rather than the alveoli.

Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram-positive, spore-forming rod with a polypeptide capsule of poly-D-glutamate that resists phagocytosis. Inhalational anthrax follows exposure to spores from contaminated animal hides or wool (woolsorters disease) or a deliberate release. Inhaled spores are ingested by alveolar macrophages and carried to mediastinal lymph nodes, where they germinate. The bacteria release toxins that share a binding component, protective antigen: edema factor, an adenylate cyclase that raises cAMP and causes edema, and lethal factor, a zinc protease that cleaves MAP kinase kinases and kills macrophages. The result is hemorrhagic necrotizing lymphadenitis and mediastinitis, seen as a widened mediastinum, often with hemorrhagic pleural effusions, after a brief flu-like phase. Shock and hemorrhagic meningitis can follow. It does not spread from person to person.

Francisella tularensis, a small gram-negative coccobacillus that survives inside macrophages, causes tularemia; as few as about 10 to 50 organisms can cause infection. Humans are infected by handling rabbits and hares, by tick or deer fly bites, or by inhaling aerosols, for example when mowing over an infected carcass. Pneumonic tularemia causes fever, cough, and patchy infiltrates with hilar nodes and pleural effusion, and the organism is a hazard to laboratory workers.

Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever. It is an intracellular bacterium with a hardy, spore-like small form that survives drying for long periods. Infected cattle, sheep, and goats shed huge numbers in placentas and birth fluids, and people inhale contaminated dust, often without direct animal contact. Acute infection causes fever, headache, atypical pneumonia, and granulomatous hepatitis; chronic infection most often causes culture-negative endocarditis.

Burkholderia pseudomallei, a gram-negative rod in soil and surface water of Southeast Asia and northern Australia, causes melioidosis. Infection follows inhalation or skin inoculation, especially in the rainy season, and diabetes mellitus is the main risk factor. It causes acute pneumonia with sepsis, chronic cavitary upper lobe disease that mimics tuberculosis, and abscesses in the liver, spleen, and prostate, and it can reactivate years after exposure.

blocks.caption: A travel, occupational, or animal history is usually the key clue.

integration.text: The organizing idea of this chapter is that host defense determines the disease. Encapsulated extracellular bacteria such as S. pneumoniae and Klebsiella are cleared by antibody, complement, and neutrophils, and they fill the alveoli with neutrophil exudate (lobar pneumonia, physiologically a shunt). Intracellular organisms that survive inside macrophages, including M. tuberculosis, the endemic fungi, and Legionella, require Th1 cells and interferon-gamma; mycobacteria and fungi form granulomas, and all are released by HIV, glucocorticoids, and TNF-alpha inhibitors. Aspergillus hyphae need neutrophils, Pneumocystis needs CD4 cells, and allergic hosts turn harmless colonization into type I and type III hypersensitivity. Mechanical defenses add the anatomy: loss of cilia (influenza, pertussis, Mycoplasma), loss of the cough and glottic barrier (aspiration, intubation), and small infant airways (RSV) explain who gets which infection.

Toxins explain disease far from the organism: diphtheria toxin stops protein synthesis in heart and nerves, pertussis toxin produces lymphocytosis by disabling Gi, and anthrax toxins act in the mediastinum. Physiology then explains the findings: consolidation causes shunt and loud transmitted sounds, alveolar wall thickening causes diffusion limitation seen on exertion, and bronchiolar plugs cause air trapping. These are general rules for reasoning; individual organisms can cross patterns, so the host, exposure, and timing should always be weighed together.

summary: Lobar pneumonia (mainly S. pneumoniae, also Klebsiella) consolidates a lobe through congestion, red and gray hepatization, and resolution, with dullness, increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, egophony, and shunt hypoxemia; bronchopneumonia (S. aureus, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas) is patchy and centered on bronchioles.

Atypical pneumonia inflames the alveolar septa, so the film looks worse than the patient; Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall and causes cold agglutinins, and Legionella from water aerosols causes high fever, diarrhea, confusion, and hyponatremia.

Diphtheria toxin, encoded by a prophage, ADP-ribosylates EF-2, forming an adherent pseudomembrane locally and causing myocarditis with heart block and demyelinating cranial and peripheral neuropathy at a distance; the Elek test proves toxin production.

Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides infect healthy hosts by inhaled conidia, are controlled by Th1 granulomas that mimic tuberculosis, and disseminate to skin, bone, and meninges when cell-mediated immunity fails.

Pneumocystis pneumonia (CD4 below about 200) causes bilateral ground-glass opacities, high LDH, and exertional desaturation from diffusion limitation; Aspergillus causes aspergilloma in old cavities, angioinvasion in neutropenia, and ABPA in asthma and cystic fibrosis.

Aspiration of oral anaerobes in reduced consciousness or dysphagia causes lung abscess with an air-fluid level and putrid sputum in dependent right lung segments; hospital and ventilator pneumonias are caused by Pseudomonas, MRSA, and enteric gram-negative rods, and chemical pneumonitis is a sterile acid injury that appears within hours.

Pertussis toxin inactivates Gi, raising cAMP and causing lymphocytosis; the disease passes through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, and young infants have apnea and pneumonia instead of a whoop.

RSV is the leading cause of infant bronchiolitis in winter, with bronchiolar plugging, wheeze, air trapping, and hypoxemia that are most severe in premature infants and those with heart or lung disease.

Primary tuberculosis forms a Ghon complex contained by Th1 caseating granulomas into latent infection; the skin test and IGRA detect sensitization only, and only the IGRA avoids BCG false positives. Reactivation favors the oxygen-rich apices with cavitation and cytokine-driven systemic symptoms, and miliary spread reaches meninges, kidneys, adrenals, and vertebrae.

SARS-CoV-2 enters through ACE2 with TMPRSS2 cleavage and causes anosmia, diffuse alveolar damage, and thrombosis; influenza causes secondary S. aureus and S. pneumoniae pneumonia and new pandemic strains by reassortment, and anthrax, tularemia, Q fever, and melioidosis are recognized by exposure history.

verify: The timing of the four stages of lobar pneumonia varies between sources and is given only approximately.
The proportion of Mycoplasma infections that produce cold agglutinins is quoted from about 50% to 75%; the chapter says about half.
The mechanism of hyponatremia in Legionella infection (SIADH, renal sodium loss, or both) is not settled; the chapter states the association only.
The onset times of diphtheritic myocarditis and of cranial and peripheral neuropathy vary between sources and are given in general terms.

Taxonomy has changed for several organisms: RSV is now in the family Pneumoviridae, Chlamydia pneumoniae is also named Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Coxiella can be grown in cell-free media although it is traditionally called obligate intracellular; confirm the names NABNE expects.
Tuberculin skin test cutoffs (5, 10, 15 mm) and the risk groups assigned to each follow CDC guidance; confirm the current version NABNE uses.
The lifetime reactivation risk of latent tuberculosis (about 5 to 10%) and the infectious dose of Francisella tularensis (about 10 to 50 organisms) are approximate values that vary by source.
Mendelson syndrome is often linked to aspirates of pH below about 2.5 and volume above about 0.3 mL/kg from early studies; these thresholds are omitted here and should be confirmed if tested.
COVID-19 risk factors and pathology reflect evidence that is still being refined, including the relative roles of direct viral injury and immune dysregulation in thrombosis.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: lobar-vs-bronchopneumonia (distribution of consolidation in the two patterns), ghon-complex (subpleural focus with hilar node), and aspiration-segments (dependent bronchopulmonary segments supine and upright).
